title: Inflammation
seo: Inflammation: Causes, Foods That Help & What Actually Works
card: What chronic inflammation is, what drives it, and the food and lifestyle changes with real evidence behind them.
intro: Inflammation is your immune system's repair crew. Short bursts heal cuts and fight germs. The problem is when it never clocks out. Here's what keeps it running, and what actually helps.
glance: Moving more, weight loss if needed
what: Inflammation is how your body reacts to injury or infection. Blood flow increases and immune cells rush in to clean up and repair. That's why a sprained ankle swells and a cut turns red.

There are two kinds. Acute inflammation is fast and short: it starts within hours and settles in days. Chronic (long-term) inflammation is low and slow: it simmers for months or years, often with no obvious symptoms.
types: Redness, heat, swelling, pain. Lasts hours to days. It's a sign your body is healing. Don't try to "fix" it with food.
Low-level and quiet. Linked with heart disease, type 2 diabetes, some cancers and joint problems. This is what lifestyle changes target.
termNote: "Chronic inflammation" isn't a diagnosis on its own. It's a process. A doctor looks for the cause, such as an infection, an autoimmune condition or a metabolic problem. Be wary of anyone who says you "have inflammation" and sells a cure in the same breath.
causes: Extra body fat, especially around the waist
Fat tissue, particularly deep belly fat, releases inflammatory signals. Higher body weight tracks with higher inflammation markers.
Smoking raises inflammation and lowers the body's natural anti-inflammatory signals. Polluted air and dust at work (like silica) add to the load.
Regular exercise lowers inflammation markers, so long stretches of inactivity leave them higher.

In conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, psoriasis or inflammatory bowel disease, the immune system attacks the body's own tissue. Some infections, like TB, can also smolder for months. These need a doctor, not a diet.
Irregular sleep and insomnia are linked with higher inflammation markers.
Ongoing physical or emotional stress triggers inflammatory signals. Depression is linked with higher CRP too.
An eating pattern high in sugar, refined flour and trans fat
Diets heavy in sugary drinks, refined carbohydrates (maida, white bread), and saturated and trans fats are linked with more inflammatory molecules.
Inflamed, bleeding gums are linked with heart disease and diabetes. The link is well documented, but it isn't yet proven that gum disease causes them.
Inflammation markers tend to creep up with age. Scientists call this "inflammaging." Staying active and keeping a healthy weight seem to slow it.
helps: Aim for 150 minutes a week of moderate activity, like brisk walking, plus muscle strengthening on 2 days. A review of 83 trials found exercise lowered CRP, even without weight loss.
Lose some weight, if you carry extra
Weight loss is the single most effective way to lower chronic inflammation. Exercise plus weight loss beat exercise alone in the trials above.
One of the biggest single changes you can make for inflammation and your heart. Ask your doctor about quit aids.

Lots of vegetables, fruit, beans, whole grains, nuts and olive oil, with fish if you eat it. In trials it lowered some inflammation markers (IL-6, IL-1β) more than other diets, though the drop in CRP wasn't clear-cut.
The CDC recommends at least 7 hours a night for adults. Steady bedtimes help too.
Yoga, meditation, a walk with a friend. Pick what you'll actually do. Stress drives inflammatory signals, and calming practices are a sensible, low-risk way to push back.
Brush, floss and see the dentist
Treating gum disease is good for your mouth for sure, and may help the rest of you.
limit: Sugary drinks, packaged juices, mithai most days
Maida-heavy snacks: white bread, biscuits, bakery items
Deep-fried foods, especially in reused oil
Processed meats like sausages and bacon
plate: Oats with walnuts and berries, or moong dal chilla with mint chutney
Rajma or chana with brown rice or roti, plus a big salad with olive oil
Roasted chana, a handful of nuts, or an apple or guava
Palak paneer or grilled fish, mixed veg sabzi, whole-wheat roti
nutrients: EPA and DHA (from fish) and ALA (from flaxseed, chia, walnuts). Trials in rheumatoid arthritis show people needed fewer painkillers, but effects on pain and swelling were inconsistent. Adults need 1.1 g (women) to 1.6 g (men) of ALA a day; 1 tbsp of flaxseed has about 2.35 g. No upper limit is set, and the FDA considers up to 5 g a day of EPA + DHA from supplements safe. High doses can increase bleeding risk, and 4 g a day was linked to a slightly higher risk of an irregular heartbeat (atrial fibrillation) in heart patients. On warfarin? Your doctor may want to check your INR.

In the large VITAL trial, 2,000 IU a day for about 5 years led to 22% fewer new autoimmune conditions (a borderline result). But vitamin D supplements don't reliably lower CRP. If you might be low, ask your doctor about testing. Upper limit: 4,000 IU a day.
High-fiber diets are linked with lower inflammation. Dals, beans, whole grains, vegetables and fruit are the easy way in.

An antioxidant found in amla, guava, citrus and peppers. Food sources are great, but there isn't good evidence that supplements lower inflammation in people who aren't low. Upper limit: 2,000 mg a day.

Another antioxidant, found in nuts, seeds and plant oils. Supplements haven't been shown to lower inflammation in people who aren't low, and they can raise bleeding risk with blood thinners like warfarin. Upper limit: 1,000 mg a day from supplements.
Your body needs them, and being low is linked with more inflammation. That doesn't mean extra pills help if your levels are fine. Get them from nuts, seeds, dals and whole grains.
claims: Turmeric supplements fix inflammation
y

Cooking with haldi is great. As supplements, turmeric and curcumin show early promise for knee osteoarthritis pain. But high-strength "bioavailable" curcumin products have been linked to liver damage, and supplements may be unsafe in pregnancy. Ask your doctor first, especially if you take medicines.
Detox teas and juice cleanses flush out inflammation
r

There's no good research that detox programs remove toxins. Any weight lost usually comes back. Some products have had hidden ingredients, and colon cleanses can cause real harm. Your liver and kidneys already do the detox job, for free.
Tomatoes, potatoes and brinjal (nightshades) cause inflammation
w
Research hasn't found that nightshades harm joints or raise inflammation. If one seems to bother you, try leaving it out for a few weeks and see.
Dairy is inflammatory
r
A review of 52 clinical trials found dairy, including curd and fermented milk, had a mildly anti-inflammatory effect overall. The exception: people with a true milk allergy.
Sugar causes inflammation
y
Partly true. A diet high in refined sugar and sugary drinks is linked with more inflammation. A sweet now and then isn't the problem; the daily pattern is.
A high CRP tells you what's wrong
r

CRP shows that inflammation is present, not where it is or why. It can be raised by a cold, an injury, smoking, poor sleep or extra weight. Your doctor interprets it alongside your symptoms and other tests.
Painkillers are a harmless daily fix
r

Regular non-aspirin NSAIDs (like ibuprofen or naproxen) can raise heart attack and stroke risk, sometimes within weeks. The FDA advises the lowest dose for the shortest time. Ongoing pain needs a doctor's visit, not a bigger bottle.
doctor: A joint is hot, red and swollen, or several joints are stiff for over an hour each morning
Fever, night sweats or weight loss you can't explain
Ongoing belly pain, diarrhea, or blood in your stool
A rash with joint pain, or tiredness that lasts more than a few weeks
Gums that bleed often or are pulling back
You use painkillers most days to get by
tests: CRP (C-reactive protein)
Shows how much inflammation is present right now, from any cause. Useful for spotting infection or tracking a known condition.
hs-CRP (high-sensitivity CRP)

Picks up small rises and is sometimes used to fine-tune heart risk. Under 1 mg/L is lower risk, 1–3 average, over 3 higher. Over 10 usually means a short-term cause, like an infection, so it's retested.
ESR (sed rate)
An older, slower marker of inflammation, often ordered with CRP.
Others your doctor may add
Blood sugar (HbA1c), cholesterol, vitamin D, or specific tests for autoimmune conditions, depending on your symptoms.
faq: What's the fastest way to lower inflammation?
There's no overnight fix. The biggest proven levers are regular exercise, losing weight if you carry extra, and not smoking. Diet and sleep add to it. Expect changes over weeks to months.
Is there an anti-inflammatory diet?

Not one official diet. The Mediterranean-style pattern has the best evidence: vegetables, fruit, dals and beans, whole grains, nuts, olive oil and fish. A typical home-cooked Indian vegetarian meal with dal, sabzi and roti fits nicely; just go easy on fried snacks and sweets.
Should I get an hs-CRP test?

It's not a routine screening test for everyone. Doctors mainly use it to fine-tune heart-risk decisions when your risk is in the middle range. Ask your doctor whether it would change anything for you.
Can I drink haldi doodh (turmeric milk) every day?
Yes, turmeric in food and drinks is fine for most people. The safety questions are about concentrated supplements, not the spice in your kitchen.
Do I need omega-3 capsules if I'm vegetarian?

Not automatically. You can meet the ALA need from ground flaxseed, chia or walnuts. Whether a fish- or algae-based EPA/DHA supplement makes sense for you is a good question for your doctor, especially if you take a blood thinner.
Does fasting or a cleanse reset inflammation?
There's no good evidence that cleanses do this, and some carry real risks. Steady habits beat short resets.

causesSub: The badge shows how strong the evidence is that each one drives inflammation.
helpsNote: Anti-inflammatory painkillers like ibuprofen and naproxen are useful for short-term pain. Taken daily for weeks, they can raise heart attack and stroke risk. If you need them most days, see a doctor.
foodsSub: No single "superfood" lowers inflammation. Your overall pattern is what counts.

title: Hormonal imbalance
seo: Hormonal Imbalance: What It Really Means, Tests & What Helps
card: "Hormonal imbalance" isn't a diagnosis. Here are the real conditions behind the label, the tests that find them, and what food can and can't do.
intro: Tired, moody, gaining weight, breaking out? The internet has one answer: "hormonal imbalance." Your doctor will want a better one. Here are the real conditions behind the buzzword, how they're tested, and where food fits in.
what: Hormones are chemical messengers. Your glands release them into the blood to tell other parts of the body what to do. Thyroid hormone sets your energy use. Insulin moves sugar into cells. Estrogen, progesterone and testosterone run periods, fertility and much more.

Hormone levels are supposed to move. They rise and fall through the day, the month and the decades. A problem is when a level is too high or too low for long enough to cause symptoms, and a blood test can usually show it.
types: Underactive or overactive thyroid, PCOS, diabetes, low testosterone with symptoms, early menopause. These have clear tests and real treatments.
Monthly cycle changes, perimenopause, a dip after a bad night's sleep. Real and sometimes rough, but not a disease. Treatment is about easing symptoms.
termNote: "Hormonal imbalance" isn't a medical diagnosis. It's a marketing umbrella, often used to sell tests, teas and "hormone balancing" programs. Symptoms like tiredness, weight gain, low mood and acne have many causes, and hormones are only some of them. A doctor's job is to find which one, if any.
causesTitle: The real conditions behind the label
causesSub: These are the conditions doctors can actually test for and treat. The two at the end are popular labels, not real diagnoses. Deep-dive pages on each are coming soon.
causes: About 4.6% of Americans aged 12 and up have it, and women far more often than men. Signs: tiredness, feeling cold, constipation, dry skin, weight gain, heavier periods. A simple blood test (TSH) finds it, and a daily pill treats it.
The opposite problem: weight loss without trying, a racing heart, shaky hands, feeling hot, anxiety and poor sleep. Also found with a TSH test.

Affects an estimated 10–13% of women of reproductive age, and up to 70% don't know they have it. Signs: irregular or missed periods, extra facial or body hair, acne, thinning scalp hair, trouble getting pregnant. It raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, so it's worth diagnosing.

Menopause is 12 months in a row without a period. The average age in the US is about 52. The years before it (perimenopause) can bring hot flashes, night sweats, irregular periods, poor sleep and mood changes. Normal, but not something you have to just put up with.

Up to 90% of women get at least one symptom before their period. About 20–30% have PMS, and 2–5% have PMDD, a severe form where mood symptoms disrupt work or relationships. Effective treatments exist.

A real condition, but much rarer than ads suggest. Diagnosis needs both symptoms (low sex drive, erection problems, low energy, loss of muscle) and low levels on two separate early-morning blood tests.
When cells stop responding well to insulin, blood sugar creeps up. Often no symptoms at first. It's closely tied to PCOS and extra belly fat, and an HbA1c test picks it up.

Not a recognized condition. The Endocrine Society says there's no evidence that stress wears out your adrenal glands. In fact, stress makes them release more cortisol, not less. The tiredness is real, though, and deserves a proper check-up.
A wellness-industry term, not a medical diagnosis. Real estrogen-related problems, like heavy bleeding or fibroids, are diagnosed and treated by name.
helpsSub: First, find the cause. Then these habits help most hormone-related conditions, strongest evidence first.
helps: Thyroid disease, diabetes and PCOS are common, testable and treatable. A guess plus a supplement can delay real treatment for years.
Lose some weight, if you carry extra

In PCOS, losing just 5–10% of your body weight can improve periods, extra hair growth, insulin resistance and heart-risk markers. It also improves blood sugar in type 2 diabetes and can ease hot flashes for some women.

Aim for 150 minutes a week of moderate activity, like brisk walking, plus muscle strengthening on 2 days. It improves insulin sensitivity, which matters a lot in PCOS and diabetes. For PMS, aerobic exercise, yoga or Pilates are reasonable to try.
Eat a balanced, mostly whole-food diet

No single "hormone diet" wins. For PCOS, studies show no clear winner between diets; the best one is the one you'll stick with. Build plates around vegetables, dals and beans, whole grains, fruit, nuts and some protein at every meal.
Short sleep disrupts appetite hormones and blood sugar control. The CDC recommends at least 7 hours a night for adults.
Talk therapy (CBT) for PMS and menopause symptoms
Cognitive behavioral therapy, a structured type of talk therapy, is recommended by ACOG for PMS and PMDD, and by The Menopause Society for hot flashes.
Smoking is linked with earlier menopause and can worsen thyroid eye problems in Graves' disease (an overactive thyroid condition). Plenty of other reasons to quit too.
helpsNote: When hormones really are off, medicines often work best: thyroid pills, metformin, menopause hormone therapy, SSRIs for PMDD, or testosterone when it's truly low. These are prescriptions, with real benefits and real risks, so they're a conversation with your doctor, not a DIY project.
foodsSub: No food "balances" hormones. But a steady pattern of these supports blood sugar, thyroid and overall health.
limit: Sugary drinks, packaged juices and mithai most days (rough on insulin)
Seaweed or kelp supplements and iodine drops (too much iodine can harm the thyroid)
Alcohol, which worsens sleep, hot flashes and PMS mood
plate: Vegetable besan chilla with curd, or oats with nuts and berries
Dal, mixed veg sabzi, 2 whole-wheat rotis and a salad
Roasted chana, a guava, or yogurt with seeds
Rajma or grilled fish, brown rice or millet, and a big serving of greens
nutrients: Your thyroid needs it to make thyroid hormone. Adults need 150 mcg a day (220 mcg in pregnancy). Easy sources: iodized salt (¼ tsp has about 78 mcg), milk, curd, eggs and fish. Vegans and people who skip iodized salt may run low. Upper limit: 1,100 mcg a day. Too much, often from kelp or iodine drops, can cause or worsen thyroid problems, especially if you have autoimmune thyroid disease.

Heavy periods are a common cause of low iron, which causes tiredness that's easy to blame on "hormones." Women 19–50 need 18 mg a day, men 8 mg. Dals, chana, palak, rajma and fortified cereals help, and vitamin C (amla, guava, lemon) boosts absorption. Upper limit: 45 mg a day. Ask your doctor to test before taking pills.

ACOG suggests calcium may ease PMS symptoms, though the evidence is low quality. Adults need 1,000 mg a day (1,200 mg for women over 50). Curd, milk, paneer, ragi and til are great sources. Upper limit: 2,500 mg a day up to age 50, then 2,000 mg.

Low vitamin D is common, and it's often mentioned for thyroid disease and PCOS. But supplements haven't been shown to fix either one. If you might be low, ask your doctor about testing. Upper limit: 4,000 IU a day.
Not a hormone fixer, but worth knowing: metformin, often used for PCOS and diabetes, can lower B12 over time. Vegetarians are at extra risk too. Ask about checking your level now and then.
Often sold for PMS, but the evidence is thin. High doses taken for months can cause nerve damage. Upper limit: 100 mg a day, and some health agencies warn about lower doses.

The thyroid has more selenium than most organs. In Hashimoto's (autoimmune hypothyroidism), selenium pills can lower antibody numbers, but there's no clear proof that people feel better. Adults need 55 mcg a day; just 1 oz (6–8) of Brazil nuts has about 544 mcg, above the 400 mcg upper limit.
A popular PCOS supplement. The 2023 international PCOS guideline says the evidence is limited, and it isn't a replacement for proven treatment. Ask your doctor before trying it.
claims: "Hormone balancing" teas, gummies and supplements fix hormones
r

There's no good evidence that any blend "balances" hormones. Some herbs in them interact with medicines, and supplements can contain ingredients that aren't on the label. If something is off, a diagnosis beats a blend.
You have "adrenal fatigue"
r

Not a recognized condition. Saliva cortisol tests used to "diagnose" it aren't reliable. Adrenal supplements may contain animal gland extracts or steroids, and stopping steroids suddenly can be dangerous. Real causes of tiredness, like anemia, thyroid problems, sleep apnea, depression or diabetes, get missed.
Seed cycling balances your cycle
w
Eating flax and pumpkin seeds in one half of your cycle, then sunflower and sesame in the other, has no published trials behind it. The seeds themselves are nutritious, so enjoy them all month.
Soy wrecks your hormones or your thyroid
r

Soy foods like tofu, edamame and soy milk are safe for most people. Research hasn't shown that normal amounts cause thyroid disease. If you take a thyroid pill, keep a steady routine and ask your pharmacist how to time it with meals.
Ashwagandha calms your hormones
y

Small studies suggest it may lower stress and help sleep a little over 6–8 weeks. But it can affect thyroid levels, has been linked to liver injury, may not be safe in pregnancy, and can interact with thyroid, diabetes, blood pressure and sedative medicines. Ask your doctor first.
"Testosterone boosters" raise your T
r
A study of 50 popular boosters found 90% claimed to raise testosterone, but fewer than 25% had any data behind the claim. Some contained vitamins and minerals above safe upper limits.
Compounded "bioidentical" hormones are safer than regular hormone therapy
r

Custom-mixed hormones aren't FDA-approved and haven't been tested in randomized trials. The Menopause Society recommends FDA-approved hormone therapy, which also comes in body-identical forms, with known doses.
Black cohosh and other herbs stop hot flashes
r
The Menopause Society doesn't recommend herbal remedies or supplements for hot flashes, as the evidence doesn't hold up. CBT, weight loss if needed, and several prescription options do work.
Biotin is harmless for hair, so it doesn't matter
y

Biotin itself is low risk, but high-dose hair, skin and nail supplements can make thyroid blood tests look like an overactive thyroid. The American Thyroid Association advises stopping biotin at least 2 days before thyroid testing. Tell your doctor about all supplements.
doctor: Periods that stop for 3 months or more (and you're not pregnant), or that are very irregular
Very heavy periods, or bleeding after menopause
New facial or body hair growth, or scalp hair thinning
Weight change, a racing heart or tiredness you can't explain
Hot flashes or mood changes that disrupt sleep, work or relationships
Mood symptoms before your period that affect daily life, or any thoughts of self-harm
Trouble getting pregnant after 12 months of trying (6 months if you're 35 or older)
Low sex drive or erection problems that persist
tests: TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone)
Usually the first thyroid test. High suggests an underactive thyroid; low suggests overactive. Free T4 and thyroid antibodies may be added. Stop biotin at least 2 days before.
HbA1c and fasting glucose
Show your average blood sugar. Important if you have PCOS, extra weight around the waist, or a family history of diabetes.
For possible PCOS
Hormone blood tests (like testosterone), sometimes an ultrasound or AMH test, plus blood sugar and cholesterol. Your doctor will also rule out thyroid and prolactin problems.
For possible low testosterone
Total testosterone, drawn early in the morning after fasting, on two different days. One low result isn't enough.
For menopause
Over 45, usually no test is needed: your symptoms and period pattern tell the story. Under 45, an FSH test may help. Saliva hormone kits aren't recommended.
Ferritin and CBC
Check for low iron and anemia, a common, fixable cause of tiredness, especially with heavy periods.
faq: Can I test my hormones at home?

Some home kits use reliable blood-spot tests for things like TSH or HbA1c. Many "full hormone panels," especially saliva tests, give numbers that aren't reliable or useful. Whatever you test, a doctor needs to interpret it with your symptoms.
Can diet alone fix a hormonal imbalance?

Diet helps a lot with insulin resistance and PCOS, especially if it leads to some weight loss. But it can't cure an underactive thyroid or reverse menopause. Think of food as a strong teammate to proper treatment, not a replacement.
What's a good diet for PCOS?
There's no single PCOS diet. Choose one you can keep up: plenty of vegetables, dals, whole grains, fruit and protein, with fewer sugary drinks and refined snacks. A dietitian can help tailor it.
Does the contraceptive pill "mess up" your hormones?

The pill changes hormone levels on purpose, that's how it works. It's also a common, effective treatment for PCOS symptoms and severe PMS. If you have side effects, talk to your doctor about other options rather than stopping suddenly.
Is weight gain in my 40s my hormones?
Partly, maybe. Perimenopause can shift where fat is stored. But muscle loss, less activity, sleep and stress usually play bigger roles. A thyroid test is reasonable if you have other symptoms.
Do men have hormonal imbalance too?

Men can have thyroid disease, diabetes and true low testosterone. Testosterone drifts down slowly with age, but most men don't need treatment. Symptoms plus two low morning tests are needed for a diagnosis.
